decision: The phone docs begin their own history: their first release is 0.1.0, and versions stay below 1.0 while the docs are still forming. The changelog and manifest inherited from the template they were made from are cleared, with a note saying whose history that was. Release-please reads its config and manifest.
why: The docs were made from text-as-data-template on 2026-11-04 and carried its history (1.0.0 to 1.2.0) as if their own; never released, release-please found no tag and proposed 1.0.0 - a claim of stability for docs days old and changing hourly. Found after landing: with no release at all, release-please treats the next as the first and gives it its own default, 1.0.0, whatever the manifest says; the config's initial-version (0.1.0) is what decides a first release.
rejected: Releasing 1.0.0 as proposed (promises what is not there); tagging 1.2.0 (it is the template's version, not the docs'); keeping the inherited changelog (it tells another repository's story as this one's).

decision: linux-phone's agents are sessions with a name, a brief kept in docs' prompts/ (bring-up, orchestration, feature-research) and places they own; their shared state is the data they already keep - backlog, decisions, research, session logs, the phone's results - read through ocoeco and drawn on the face, not a tracker of their own. An orchestration session tends the conveyor and the agents: it checks the ways by measuring hand-work, turns every rule it can into a mechanism (devlab's hold, Claude Code command hooks, CI), keeps the face fluent, and starts a research session per hard feature. Research parallelises; changes to the one phone are queued through bring-up.
why: The author, 2026-11-17, asked for an orchestrating agent, per-feature agents, perhaps an agents-orchestration repository, and the most efficient organisation found by research. Read: the Craft apps' fleet (ownership by subsystem, rules kept once, an oracle gating progress), Gas Town (work state in git, agents as identities), Anthropic (few well-bounded workers, parallel only when independent, ~15x tokens), Claude Code (hooks enforce, sessions and schedules run). Our ecosystem already holds most of it; what was missing was roles, briefs and enforcement.
rejected: A new agents-orchestration repository now (the agents' runner and its redesign live in creation-guidelines/lab-agent as oco-agent, and how-we-work under creation-guidelines; a third place would be one nature under three names - what is linux-phone's stays in docs, what every project shares goes to oco-agent when it is general); a tracker beside ocoeco such as Beads (two records of one work); an always-on watching agent (tokens without end - patrols on a schedule and hooks do it cheaper); one agent per feature implementing in parallel (one phone: changes race).

decision: No more agents for now; the conveyor session retires and hands everything to orchestration, which becomes the one session the author talks to; bring-up runs as one session per part, ended when the part lands and the next started fresh from the data; research sessions run one or two at a time, the next (sensors) only after deep-sleep shows the research brief works; the most capable model where judgment is the point (bring-up, research decisions), lighter ones for patrols and routine conveyor fixes.
why: Measured over ~80 minutes on 2026-11-17: the conveyor files results by itself (devlab 12 landings); the phone queues every change, so only research parallelises; 4 sessions on the most capable model already run, and multi-agent work costs about 15 times the tokens of one (Anthropic); a session that runs long re-reads its whole context every turn - the conveyor session's was the longest; collisions came from many hands landing in docs at once (2 of 5 gatherings failed, healed by the next boot). The author asked for the most effective organisation, not the largest.
rejected: More agents per feature now (one phone queues their changes; the research brief is unproven); keeping the conveyor session beside orchestration (two owners of one thing, the costliest context); one long-lived bring-up session (its context grows with every part).

decision: A part's status is derived (derive/support-status.sql, run through tad after every filing): broken where the latest run fails it; works where a test that proves the part does its work passed and none failed; otherwise what a person judged (judged, with the notes as its evidence). Each row says what the suite saw of the part and in which run (measured, measured_run); the tests table says what each test's pass proves - present or works.
why: The author, 2026-11-17: support status read off the suite's results, not typed. Tried beside the hand-written status first: read naively (a pass is works, nothing measured is unknown) it disagreed on 8 of 19 parts - a pass that only shows a part is there (the jack detector, Bluetooth powered, the modem seen, the NFC controller) is not the part working, and an absent measurement is no evidence against what was witnessed (the microphone's tries, fastboot). With proofs told apart, the rule and the judgment say the same on all 19.
rejected: Status typed by hand alone (it lags the phone: nothing turned it broken when a part failed); a pass read as works (would have called calls, SMS and NFC working with no SIM and no tag ever read); a measurement-less part read as unknown (would erase what was witnessed).

decision: linux-phone's pages (linux-phone-oco.github.io/docs) are its face, drawn in this place's CI from its open database: tad keeps and checks the data here; the family's other places are observed as the Linux Phones lens gathers them; the observatory's engine draws the face from that; tad's page of every table stands beside it under tables/. A landing here draws it again, and the clock every three hours, for what the other places land.
why: The author, 2026-11-17: the observatory's Linux Phones pages reflected real progress from CI and should be linux-phone's own face, with tad as the open database shared by the whole project, devlab filing the suite's results into it and the pages reflecting them - nobody drawing them by hand.
rejected: A copy of the observatory's pages kept here (a second renderer to drift); publishing from the lens's place (the database and its readers would live apart, and docs' address is the one already linked); the plain table index alone (it drew rows, not progress).

decision: The core of the project - making each part of a phone work - runs as its own session beside the conveyor's, from prompts/bring-up.md: it owns the kernel, the phone's hardware data, the upstream queue and the Sxmo profiles; the conveyor's session owns lab-tools, device-template and the face. Anything that changes the phone's state is done holding one lock (flock on ~/.local/state/devlab/CODENAME/phone.lock); each session works in clones of its own.
why: The author, 2026-11-17, asked for a parallel session on the actual core: research, reverse engineering, patches, delivered through the conveyor and proven by the suite. One phone and shared clones are where two sessions would undo each other (two jobs in one clone once merged each other's changes under one commit).
rejected: One session doing both (the conveyor kept pulling attention from the parts, and parts from the conveyor); two sessions without a lock or owners (a reboot under a kernel try, a reset clone).

decision: devlab kernel install refuses a kernel that is not an EFI executable.
why: The bootloader starts EFI programs only; a gzip kernel was lost before it could log a line.
rejected: Documenting which file to pass.

decision: devlab health waits until the phone has been up 90 seconds before checking, saying so once.
why: Every job slept before a health check by hand (7 times); a check read too early fails for the wrong reason.
rejected: A fixed sleep in every script; checking at once and retrying failures.

decision: A listening test runs only with --placed, the word that the microphone is by the phone.
why: The first results came from a microphone being worn.
rejected: Un-naming the microphone's file as the safeguard: a trick only its author remembers.

decision: devlab kernel try waits for a new boot id and reports the outcome itself, judged from the running release, the entry's counter and the timeout log.
why: Booting a test kernel and reading what happened was the heaviest manual work (9 times, 54 effort-minutes), and guessing at it cost three reboots.
rejected: Waiting for the phone to go down and then up (it misfired twice: the try schedules its reboot); leaving the reading to a person.

decision: A change devlab makes to the phone ends with its health: after a reboot (phone reboot, kernel try) devlab waits for the report that boot writes by itself, rather than running the suite again; after a change without a reboot (provision) it runs the suite now. Either way the report is brought to the lab and an unhealthy phone fails the command.
why: Nobody has to remember to check; and waiting for the boot's own report measures exactly what every boot of the phone measures - the lab adds no second way of checking.
rejected: Running the suite from the lab after each reboot (two runs per boot, and the lab's run would be the one that differs from an unattended boot); leaving the health check as a separate step to remember.

decision: devlab files the phone's reports into the picture through tad (one tad sql statement per run: its rows read from the report, its counts from those rows; tad keeps it only if every rule holds, then canonical form and the rendered pages), and devlab watch, after every boot, waits for the phone's own report, says its verdict on the board, and gathers with --land: in devlab's own clones of the lab and the picture, each landed through land, signed devlab. The face is drawn again by the picture's CI on that landing.
why: The author, 2026-11-17: tad is the open database shared by the whole linux-phone project; devlab reports the suites' results into it by itself and the pages reflect them - not an agent doing it by hand each time. devlab's own clones keep its landings out of the clones people and agents work in (two hands in one clone once merged each other's changes).
rejected: devlab appending JSON lines itself (rows tad never checked); the watch running the lab-side checks over SSH (a second way of measuring beside the phone's own); landing from ~/Projects (collides with work in progress there).

decision: devlab gather now brings every report the phone keeps that the lab lacks into the device lab's tests/results (RUN.jsonl, as written on the phone), and files every run not yet filed into linux-phone-oco/docs' test_results and test_runs, the rows made from the report's lines. A run is filed once, by its id.
why: Filing was by hand (tests/to-docs.sh, through tad's Python) and had fallen a week behind: docs held 7 runs from 2026-11-10 while the lab had made many since. Rust carries it now, and the tables stay where they are declared and observed today.
rejected: Declaring test_runs and test_results again in each device lab (one nature, two declarations - entered as the sign a-test-run-has-no-shared-shape in ocoeco, to be answered in the language); keeping to-docs.sh (new filing through Python).

decision: The phone measures its own health after every boot: devlab-health, a static Rust runner, runs small check files (base layer, then shell layer) and writes one report per run in test_results' shape, keeping the evidence when unhealthy. The checks are POSIX shell in postmarketOS's test shape and print plain words (pass|fail|skip TEST COMPONENT detail); the runner makes the JSON, the verdict and the evidence. Generic checks live in lab-tools; what a phone is expected to have is its manifest's [health], and a phone's own checks sit beside the generic ones.
why: Health measured only from the lab is health only while the lab is connected and remembers to ask; a phone that checks itself after every boot leaves a record for every change. Shipped code is Rust (2026-11-11-rust-for-what-ships): strings and structure - JSON escaping, the report - are where shell is fragile. The probes themselves only read sysfs and the system's own tools, which is what postmarketOS's tests and bootrr do in shell, so they can be contributed there.
rejected: A shell runner (JSON escaping and report shaping in sh - the fragility the Rust decision answers); checks written in Rust (a probe of sysfs gains nothing, and upstream would not take it); keeping the checks run only from the lab over SSH (no record when the lab is not asking); one check file per device (surya's checks.sh: nothing reusable for the next phone).

decision: The health suite reaches phones as an Alpine package (devlab-health: the runner, the checks, the unit and the timer) published through the package conveyor once it publishes Alpine repositories (cv-apk); until then devlab puts the same files on the phone itself, as the development path.
why: The commons has one packaging conveyor that every project calls (linux-package-distribution-oco/conveyor) and it already builds aarch64-musl binaries; a package is how postmarketOS installs and updates anything, and it gives the phone updates the way the lab machine already gets them.
rejected: devlab copying files onto the phone for good (a second delivery route beside the conveyor; nothing updates it); building the package in lab-tools' own CI (copying what the conveyor exists to do once).

decision: Every test sound is quiet unless the phone's manifest says otherwise: [hear] level_dbfs (default -40 dBFS) and volume (default 25%), capped at full scale and 100%, used by devlab hear and given to every check through the phone's health.env (TEST_TONE_DBFS, TEST_VOLUME).
why: The author, 2026-11-17, urgently: a full-scale test sine played at night; test sounds must be quiet, with a setting for it in the suite. devlab hear had -12 dBFS at 60% volume hard-coded.
rejected: Lowering the hard-coded numbers (no setting, and other checks would choose their own); a level per check (a phone in a home has one acceptable loudness).

decision: devlab holds the phone for every change it makes - flash, provision, reboot, root commands, put, kernel install, try and remove, suite put - by an exclusive lock on STATE/phone.lock, from the command line and the MCP door alike; a second change waits for the first and says so. Reading needs no hold.
why: Two sessions now work with one phone (the bring-up session beside the conveyor's): a reboot under a kernel try would strand a test or misreport it. A lock each session must remember to take is a rule kept by care; devlab taking it itself is kept by the tool.
rejected: flock around devlab by convention (forgotten once is enough; and wrapped around a devlab that also locks, it would wait on itself); a lock only in the MCP door.

decision: devlab offers its structured door over MCP (devlab mcp, stdio, with rmcp): run, put and get a file, the health report, kernel install, try and status, reboot and wait - each the same function the command line calls.
why: Agent access plans every tool's structured door over MCP in Rust with rmcp, devlab among the first (aa-two-doors); an agent then works with the phone without a person and without a shell's quoting layer.
rejected: A separate MCP server project beside devlab (two doors to keep in step); MCP through a generic shell tool (every call a quoting puzzle).

decision: The ways an agent must keep on the lab (land, not a push to main; no Python; the phone only through devlab) are held by Claude Code command hooks that call devlab guard, a subcommand of devlab in Rust, with its cases tested.
why: A way that must be remembered is forgotten; the hook refuses when it is tried and says why, to the agent that tried. devlab already knows the phones (their manifests and learned addresses), so the guard knows what reaching the phone means.
rejected: Hook scripts in shell with jq (logic in shell, untested; the guide says Rust for logic); a separate guard tool beside devlab (a second place that must learn the phones addresses); permission deny rules in settings (match command prefixes only: miss sudo, env, sh -c and $(...), and cannot tell a branch push from a push to main).

decision: A device lab made from this template holds data only - the manifest, the phone's own checks, its reports, its records; every tool is devlab's and reads the manifest.
why: The design asked for 2026-11-10 (linux-phone-oco/docs backlog device-template): the next phone must not inherit a copy of surya's scripts to edit; surya-lab already shows where copies drift (its shell tools and devlab doing the same work twice).
rejected: Copying surya-lab and renaming (the scripts would drift per phone); a template carrying its own scripts beside devlab (two routes to the same work).

decision: For linux-phone-oco, everything goes through tad in one database: linux-phone-oco/docs. The records its places kept in ocoeco's oco/ tables (lab-tools, surya-lab, device-template, sxmo-deviceprofiles) are docs' tables now, each row naming its place in project (full id, linux-phone-oco/NAME); docs' mark holds those places, so on the face each record stays its place's. Every record is written through tad's named records kept in docs (records/NAME.sql: tad r decision|backlog|backlog-status|research|session-log|concept|source|milestone-readiness --project NAME ...), read through named queries (queries/), and the feeds, the status derivation and devlab's filing of a run are named records too. The record of work is git itself: linux-phone places export no glimpses, land asks for none, landit makes none, devlab's landings carry none; commits are signed by the name a session works under (oco-work sets the git author to OCOECO_BY), and the face reads where each hand stands off the commits (bin/landings.sh, landings) after the glimpse history kept in docs. Sub-repositories' marks shrink to the mark itself, pointing here. The face keeps its CI (observe through linux-phone-oco/lens, drawn by the engine); drawing it straight from this database waits until observing becomes a burden. ocoeco stays as it is for the rest of the commons.
why: The author, 2026-11-17: for linux-phone everything goes through tad in one database, and the record of work is git itself. Measured friction behind it: the turn commit-title limit failed 4 times; refusals of links pointing nowhere ordered the work 3 times; and two tools (ocoeco note and tad) wrote rows in one place - docs' decisions, problems and glimpses were ocoeco's files beside tad's tables, undeclared, and appended glimpse lines conflicted between sessions landing at once (seen again on 2026-11-17 in lab-tools). Checked before the old way was retired: every row of every place is in docs (lab-tools 110 with glimpses, surya-lab 99, device-template 12, sxmo-deviceprofiles 10, lens 3), the 25 tables the face reads observe the same, and the face rendered from both is the same page for page but for each mark's count of shared tables.
rejected: Keeping ocoeco note beside tad (two tools writing one database - the overlap this ends); one database per sub-repository (one nature kept in five places); retiring ocoeco everywhere (the author's observatory rests on it, and it was not asked); a new 'ocotad' command line over the database (a second tool over one database: tad's named statements say the same as files beside the data); queries compiled into tad (each new one would need a release of tad, where a file lands with the work that needs it); drawing the face from this database now (its CI works; not before observing is a burden).

decision: devlab-health reaches phones as an Alpine package: release-plz tags devlab-health-vX.Y.Z, and the package conveyor's alpine.yml builds it from the tag's APKBUILD, signs it with lab-tools' own RSA key, verifies it and publishes an apk repository on lab-tools' pages for postmarketOS v26.06 (Alpine 3.24), then installs it in a clean container.
why: One way for code to reach a phone, measured, instead of devlab copying files: the phone updates the suite with the rest of its system, and any postmarketOS phone can take it without the lab. The conveyor already did this for pacman; the Alpine path was its open cv-apk.
rejected: Keeping devlab suite put as the only way (files no package manager knows, nothing for a phone outside the lab); building in lab-tools' own CI (copying what the conveyor keeps once); a key shared across the commons (keys stay per project for now); publishing as release assets (apk needs an index under a stable path).

decision: Calls on surya are made to work as pulpoff/linux-surya carries them - q6voice from sdm845-mainline with SM7150's CVD 2.3 set-up and a hostless VoiceMMode1 link in our kernel, then UCM Voice Call with TX topology 0x10F70 and a 1-channel uplink capture on TX_CODEC_DMA_TX_3 - and proven by the phone itself calling blueSIP's public echo line (+49 89 721010 99701): three tones played on the loudspeaker are heard by the bottom mic going up and again, a round trip later, coming back on the earpiece, found by Goertzel envelopes in a Rust subcommand of devlab-health. Its tone line (99702) proves the downlink alone; the SIM's own mailbox is the fallback. At most one call of 25 s a day; skipped as unknown without a SIM, a registration or the call path. Mobile data is checked every boot over the bearer's own interface (registration, DNS, pings, 100 kB), with a weekly 5 MB throughput run, under 0.3 GB a month. The first step is the kernel: q6voice and the VoiceMMode1 link, settled by the check call-audio-path, which fails today.
why: An independent mainline tree on this very phone already carries calls with sound both ways, so the biggest unknown is porting, not discovery; the check call-audio-path settles it without a SIM or a call. The echo line is the only public German echo attested across years and sources, and costs a landline-rate call; its tone line splits a failure into downlink and uplink. The acoustic loop proves exactly what a person uses - loudspeaker, mic, uplink, network, downlink, earpiece - and needs no driver feature beyond what calls need anyway (the uplink capture is written to a file instead of discarded). Daily and short keeps the cost to cents and the people reached to none.
rejected: Digital loop through in-call record/playback ports (unknown whether sdm845-mainline's q6voice has them; kept for later if it does). A second phone on a stand that answers (hardware and a second SIM; the echo line does the same for nothing). A programmable number (Twilio and the like: an account, money, a public endpoint). sipgate's echo 10005 (SIP-internal, not dialable from a mobile, private customers dropped 2025). Old or foreign echo lines (portunity 0211, sip2sip +31, C*NET: unconfirmed, international rates). Calling the author's other phone as the automatic test (reaches a person; stays the half-manual mode of 2026-11-11-telephony-checks). Downstream's 0x10F71 topology (silence without Xiaomi's calibration). A call on every boot (45 a day in bring-up).

decision: The phones' health suites keep one contract - a check prints 'pass|fail|skip TEST COMPONENT detail', and docs' tests table says what a pass proves - and two languages by kind of work: shell for readings (sysfs, a command's output, a few readable lines on BusyBox), and Rust for anything with numbers, timing or states (tones, echoes, calls, sleep counters), as subcommands of one static multi-call binary shipped with devlab-health (devlab-health tone make|find, later call echo), unit-tested on the lab with recorded fixtures and cross-built by health/build.sh. rust-script is the lab's tool for prototypes and one-off analysis of recordings fetched from the phone; a prototype that is kept becomes a subcommand. Checks are layered by cost: base, shell, telephony (calls and data, budgeted, at most daily), witnessed (a person). Coverage is a query over docs: every device's components with no test proving works.
why: The shell contract is what makes a check quick to write and read, and it already runs everywhere; what goes wrong in shell is arithmetic - three of surya's checks carry an awk Goertzel and a printf-built tone that nobody unit-tests, while lab-tools' tone crate has tests and never reaches the phone. The phone has no Rust toolchain, so Rust must arrive compiled; one binary already goes there (devlab-health), so analysis joins it at no new cost. rust-script works today on the lab; Cargo's own scripts are still nightly-only (Cargo 1.99 asks for -Zscript) and can replace rust-script when they are stable.
rejected: Python checks (refused on the lab; the phone's python3 is the image's, not ours). rust-script or cargo script on the phone (a toolchain and network on the phone, minutes of compiling at boot). Every check in Rust (a ten-line sysfs reading becomes a cross-build per change). bats or another shell test framework (bash, not BusyBox ash; the contract already does its work). LAVA or a KTAP-native harness now (a lab of many boards; our lines map onto KTAP if ever needed). One binary per check (many cross-builds and files to ship).

decision: An expert is a domain written down in docs, not a session kept alive. Each hard domain (audio, sleep, modem, sensors, cameras) is its component's rows - research, decisions, backlog, tests, sources - plus one research row per domain, DOMAIN-how-it-stands, that holds the tacit part (dead ends, where experiments live, what to never do again), added to item by item, never rewritten whole. A session takes up a domain by its brief and that domain's rows, and becomes its expert by reading them. It is ended when its part lands, or before its context is compacted, after writing its hand-over into those rows (not into notes outside the repository); the next starts fresh from them. Questions route by the record first: whoever asks reads the domain's rows; if they do not answer, they message the domain's live session directly (the face shows where each hand stands), not through orchestration; with no live session, orchestration starts a short read-only consult from the domain's rows on a lighter model, and every answer is written back as a row. One writer per domain and one hand on the phone (devlab) stay as they are.
why: Measured here: sessions grow to 1000-1800 messages and re-read them every turn; multi-agent work costs about 15 times one agent; a phone serialises all bring-up. Outside: compaction loses what only later proves to matter and summaries collapse; long contexts recall worse; relayed questions play telephone; every system that keeps experts across time (Gas Town, Anthropic's harness, Claude Code's agent memory, Letta) keeps the expertise outside the session. The author's aim - knowledge that does not depend on anyone remembering - is practice 1 of the ways.
rejected: Standing expert sessions per domain: idle hours lose the cache, so each question re-reads a thousand-message context at full price; the expertise still vanishes at compaction or when the app's session ends; their context rots with length. Orchestration as the router of every question: a bottleneck and a game of telephone (LangChain), and it fills orchestration's own context. Claude Code subagent memory (.claude/agent-memory) or agent teams as the home: a second store beside docs' one database (decision 2026-11-17-one-database), and teams do not survive a resume. A Markdown expert-notes file per domain: a second place for what rows already hold; kept only if a lens cannot show it. A vector or memory service (Letta, Hindsight): outside the commons and opaque to the face. Forking a finished expert's whole session to consult it (Cognition's smart friend): kept as an exception for a session a few hours old whose tacit context is not yet written, not the rule.

decision: devlab-health takes analysis as subcommands of its own binary: tone make|find (lab-tools' tone crate, linked with only its wav feature) and data plan|spent (the month's mobile-data ledger, a JSON file in /var/lib/devlab/health-data that pruning never touches). Their arguments are parsed by hand, and each prints one JSON line with exit 0/1/2. A check reads that line with lib.sh's json_field. mobile-data runs every boot in the telephony layer and is bounded by the month's budget, not by once_a_day. It measures the connected bearer that carries a default route and is not IMS. The week's 5 MB run counts as made only when its download came whole.
why: The tone crate already had tests, and the checks' awk Goertzel had none. Linking the crate costs 64 KiB on the phone, against two copies of the arithmetic. hound was already the lab's WAV reader, so one read_mono now serves tone, devlab hear and the runner instead of three. The research (mobile-data-check-budget) measures data every boot and bounds it by a monthly ledger; a byte count kept across runs is state, which the shell-and-Rust decision puts in Rust. On surya an IMS bearer (APN ims, IPv6, no route) sits beside the data bearer, and the first-connected rule measured it as 0 of 5 pings.
rejected: clap in devlab-health (size on the phone; argenv is the commons' parser, and moving the runner onto it is its own change). A WAV reader written again by hand (hound is there and tested). Ledger arithmetic in shell (state and numbers, against the shell-and-Rust decision). once_a_day for mobile data (the research measures every boot; the budget already bounds the cost). The first connected bearer (picked IMS on surya). Marking the weekly run as made when it failed (a broken run would hide throughput for a week).

decision: devlab guard keeps only the phone's way: ssh, scp, sftp, rsync and sshpass to a phone outside devlab are refused (devlab guard tool, PreToolUse). The ways every project shares - no git push to main, no Python, the practices and the inbox at session start - moved to the ideal-agent plugin's hooks (grenudi/ideal-agent), installed on the lab; devlab guard start is gone and the lab's settings keep only the PreToolUse hook (lab-tools #65).
why: The author, 2026-11-17: general agent know-how has one home, grenudi/ideal-agent (its decision 2026-11-17-one-home-for-agent-know-how). Held in devlab, the shared rules held only on the lab. Before devlab's rules were removed, both guards were given the same 19 events: they agreed on every push and Python case; the one difference was the phone's, which stays here.
rejected: Both guards holding the shared rules (two guards saying one thing drift apart). Moving the phone's rule to the plugin too (it is this lab's device: its addresses come from devlab's state).

decision: The briefs in prompts/ keep only what is linux-phone's - what a role owns, its places, devlab and the phone, recording in docs - and name the skill for the method from the ideal-agent plugin: orchestrate-agents, research-a-feature, bring-up-a-part, with lab-session-start, land-a-change, record-the-work and change-a-device. The general research and decisions on how agents are organised (landscape photocraft-fleet, gas-town, anthropic-multi-agent, claude-code-agents; decisions 2026-11-17-agents-organised-by-the-data and -experts-written-not-standing) are carried into ideal-agent as its own; the rows here stay as linux-phone's.
why: The author, 2026-11-17: one home for general agent know-how (grenudi/ideal-agent), each project's docs keeping the domain-specific knowledge, so both improve in their own place.
rejected: Keeping the whole method in each brief (copies drift between projects); deleting the linux-phone rows that were carried over (they are linux-phone's history and decisions, cited by its own records).

decision: surya has one keeper: the one session that owns the phone's flow, taking up the phone's queue one change at a time; devlab still holds the phone for each change. The keeper is a role filled by successive fresh sessions: each takes a lease (devlab keeper take), reads how the phone stands (tad q phone-stands, the last keeper's hand-over) and the queue (tad q phone-queue: backlog items marked needs=phone, each with the test that proves it; also on the face), works to proofs, writes how the phone stands and ends when its piece lands or its context grows large. Research, expert and conveyor sessions never change the phone; they put work on its queue. A waker (a scheduled task on the lab) becomes the keeper when the queue has work and the lease is free. The brief is docs ideal-agent-linux-phone-oco/phone-keeper.md, the domain part of ideal-agent's keeper of a shared resource. Bring-up's role becomes the phone keeper's.
why: The author, 2026-11-17 ('yes, hand it over'): one owner of the phone, always taking the next thing it needs, filled by successive sessions. The bring-up session had grown to about 1,770 messages: a session held as the phone's long memory is slow and costly, while the phone's state and work are already data. devlab's hold makes each change safe but says nothing of what comes next; a queue read off the backlog does, and research sessions had no way to hand the phone work but a message.
rejected: Bring-up as one long-lived session (its context grows without end, and the phone's knowledge lives in a conversation); several sessions changing the phone in turn without an owner (devlab serialises changes, not intentions - experiments interleave); a separate queue table (one nature in two places - the backlog already holds the work; needs and proof are two fields on it); a lock of our own around devlab (it would wait on itself; the lease says who keeps the phone, not who holds it for a change); a waker that starts a second session beside a live keeper (the lease refuses the second).

decision: Where it stands (2026-11-17): accepted. The author accepted the corrected design the same day ('looks clean, i like it', said of this decision as it stood after docs #174, relayed by the conveyor session). Landed: the about link and the about query (docs #170) and the agent folder (docs #171). Open as work, waiting on no one: building idealkb (idealkb-from-template, its own session) and the short entry (kb-entry). The decision, as corrected by the author: tad stays what it is - a database, transparent, workable in SQL, at ease in git and displayable - and how to organise a knowledge base is written once, in a new repository, grenudi/ideal-knowledge-base (idealkb), which uses tad as its database by pinning tad's release and grows on top of it what a knowledge base needs. (1) The rule of file and table: a thing there are many of with one shape, that is cited, linked, dated or changes state, is a row (decision, research, source, backlog, session log, concept, test, status, word); prose read once in order is a file (README, AGENTS.md, a brief, an essay too long for a row, kept in research/ and cited by a row); rendered pages are output for people and the face, never what an agent reads to answer; the named statements are the base's interface. (2) The about link: every record table names what it is about in one field, checked by a references rule against the base's subjects - Wikidata's statement about an item. (3) The generic statements every base gets: queries about SUBJECT, next, find TEXT (ids and first lines only), row ID and recent; records with --about. (4) One entry: AGENTS.md under 3 KB, with CLAUDE.md as @AGENTS.md - what the base is in two lines, an orientation table from typical question to the command that answers it, tad statements for everything else, and the rule: never read data/ or docs/ to answer, ask a query. (5) The standing record tables: backlog, session_log, decisions, research (with sources). (6) Its own tad base describing itself. A base follows idealkb by a pinned release, as it pins tad: the weekly pin job keeps the generic declaration, statements and entry current, landing only where the base's CI passes; a base's own change to a generic file shows as a diff in that job's pull request, the signal to send it upstream. Starting a bare tad database belongs to tad itself - for example a tad init in place of the template's scaffold - general to any database, with nothing of a domain. text-as-data-template hands its pieces to those two (the scaffold to tad, the standing tables to idealkb), its reasons are carried into their records before it goes (Chesterton's fence: what each piece was for, from its session_log), and it is retired with a pointer. How an agent finds its way in any base is a skill of ideal-agent; ideal-project-playbook keeps the process and points to idealkb for its backlog, development-log and idea templates, and its findability test becomes idealkb's measure. In linux-phone-oco/docs the root stays the base, and the agent specifics are in ideal-agent-linux-phone-oco/ (done). For later only: tad's README keeps rendering in tad until it moves to a tool of its own; by this split it belongs eventually with the knowledge base and the face.
why: The author, 2026-11-17: one general place for how to organise a knowledge base, used by every base; agents find what they need instead of reading everything; don't reinvent the wheel, don't make it more cumbersome. Corrected by him the same day: tad stays a database, and idealkb uses it as its database and grows a knowledge base on top. This agrees with tad's own record - its whole concern is the data, and what is done with the data belongs to the tools that use it (2026-11-12-tad-is-text-as-data). The template is tad's starter from the vendored era (a Python .tad/ copied in by git subrepo, plus standing backlog and session_log tables); renamed into idealkb, it would have folded a database's scaffold into a knowledge base. Measured (kb-navigation-measured): the weight was a missing subject link, not the size of the entry. The world's practice agrees (kb-organisation-world); the commons' overlaps are in kb-organisation-commons.
rejected: Growing idealkb by renaming text-as-data-template (this decision's first form): it would fold a database's scaffold into a knowledge base; the author corrected it. The first form's rejection of 'a new idealkb beside the template' no longer applies: once the template is split between tad and idealkb, nothing remains beside it. Putting the knowledge-base layer into tad: tad's concern is the data alone (2026-11-12-tad-is-text-as-data). Folding it into ideal-project-playbook: the playbook is how to run a software project, and a base is not one. Folding it into ideal-agent: a base is read by people and the face too; ideal-agent keeps only the navigation skill. Moving docs' database into a subfolder named ideal-knowledge-base-linux-phone-oco: devlab's filing, tad's working directory, GitHub Pages' docs/, the mark's exports and every link to a row's page stand on the root. A copied template: copies drift, as this one has. A spec document alone: nothing checks that a base follows it. A plugin skill as the vehicle: only Claude agents would get it. llms.txt as the agent's entry: it serves outside readers of a site. Embeddings or a vector index: 4k rows are answered exactly by a checked link and named queries. A table of questions naming their queries: a second index to keep true. A folder per Diataxis kind or PARA bucket: the tables already sort by kind.

decision: docs is ideal-knowledge-base's first follower: idealkb.toml pins release 0.1.0, the generic queries next, find, row and recent are idealkb's, and AGENTS.md is the short entry - two lines on what docs is, linux-phone's own questions (phone-queue, phone-stands, coverage, a place's records, the agent folder), and idealkb's generic part between idealkb:begin and idealkb:end. docs keeps as its own: its about query (it also reads the support matrix, feature support and the tests), its records (they take --project: one database of several places) and tables.toml (its standing tables carry project, needs and proof). The editing recipes moved to CONTRIBUTING.md whole.
why: Decision 2026-11-17-ideal-knowledge-base, accepted by the author; backlog kb-entry and idealkb-from-template. A base's extensions named as own are not overwritten by the weekly pin job, which says when idealkb changes one of them.
rejected: Taking idealkb's records and about query (they would drop --project and the support matrix: docs' own CI and devlab's filing stand on them); renaming docs' queries to fit (every link and brief naming tad q about would break); deleting the recipes from AGENTS.md (they are still how the data is edited - they belong in CONTRIBUTING.md, which a person reads to change it); moving the base into a subfolder (devlab's filing, Pages and the mark stand on the root - the decision's own rejection).

decision: linux-phone's face is drawn from docs' own data: bin/face-data makes the engine's data from docs' tables (each row naming its place), the lens kept in docs' face/ (lens.toml, its translations and log, moved from linux-phone-oco/lens), each place's mark (oco.toml) and what GitHub says the work made (commits of 90 days, each workflow's latest run, releases); the engine (oco site) draws it as before. ocoeco observe and the lens checkout left pages.yml (docs #182), and no brief has an ocoeco step: the whole is read through docs' named queries and the face.
why: The author, 2026-11-17: linux-phone must not depend on ocoeco. Since docs holds every linux-phone record in one tad database, observing the family through ocoeco only re-gathered what docs already keeps. Checked before landing: drawn from both, the same 120 pages; outside the build time only 16 differ, and only where the new data is fuller - activity counts every place's commits (393 in 90 days, not docs' 186), releases show (observe found none), every workflow's latest run shows. Proven on the live face after landing.
rejected: Keeping ocoeco observe (another project's tool to read our own data); the face drawn by tad render alone (it renders tables, not the face's views - matrices, paths, the queue; the engine does those); a Rust step for the data now (jq, yq and gh do it in a page of shell, as the CI step it is - a Rust step when it grows logic); keeping the lens in its own repository (a second place for the face's one definition); renaming OCOECO_BY (only a variable's name; oco-work and land read it across the ecosystem).

decision: docs follows idealkb 0.3.0: a subject's answer leads with its summary (tad r summary), condensed records by id; tad q about says where a summary is due. docs' own about query, research record and tables.toml take summaries, material and supersedes the way idealkb's do, keeping docs' status, feature, concept and test rows always in full. Research material lives in research/SUBJECT/YYYY-MM-DD/, named by its row; the Open Handset Commons model is the first, moved under its date. The session that records into a subject renews its summary when due; a keeper at hand-over.
why: The author, 2026-11-17: a subject's answer must not grow without bound, and research must be kept without loading every agent's start (idealkb decisions 2026-11-17-summary-layer and 2026-11-17-research-aside). Measured: audio-mic from 15.9 KB to 4.8 KB.
rejected: Summarising the domains' how-it-stands research rows in place: they are itemised hand-overs (decision 2026-11-17-experts-written-not-standing), records the summary condenses, not the summary itself. Condensing status, tests and concepts too: they are short, standing facts a reader needs every time. Writing all four due summaries now: each belongs to the session that knows its domain; this change proves the layer on one.

brief: Each phone has a lane coordinator that starts and renews its keepers; a scheduled task only nudges it
decision: A lane coordinator per phone (surya-coordinator) is a visible session in the sidebar: it starts the phone keepers itself, continues or replaces each when it reports, archives finished ones, and routes what needs the author's hands to the top coordinator. The scheduled task linux-phone-keeper-waker only sends it 'continue' when the queue has work and no keeper is live.
why: The author wants every running piece visible in the sidebar, and a keeper's parent receives its reports automatically; the top coordinator then coordinates coordinators.
rejected: A hidden scheduled waker that does the keeper's work itself (invisible, no parent to receive reports); the top coordinator starting keepers itself (one session for every lane, its context swamped).

brief: One health suite, lpoco-health, on the phone: upstreamable shell tests in pmOS's shape, our runner; conditions detected at run time; switches with reasons; docs keep only facts and results
decision: linux-phone-oco has one health suite, lpoco-health (devlab-health renamed; same checks, same test_results shape, same report on the phone). It keeps the shape decision 2026-11-17-health-on-the-phone chose: small shell checks printing 'pass|fail|skip TEST COMPONENT detail' (postmarketOS's test shape, so a check can later become a postmarketos-test-* subpackage by a merge request), gathered by our static Rust runner. New: (1) detected conditions - conditions/*.sh work out no-sim, no-modem, no-network at every run; checks say skip_on NAME and report 'skip: no SIM card'; nothing is written down. (2) chosen switches - lpoco-health off TEST --reason WORDS [--by], on TEST, list, kept in /etc/lpoco-health/switches (test, reason, who, when), reported as 'skip: switched off: reason (by who, when)'; never without a reason; from the lab devlab suite off|on|list and the MCP tools health_switch_off/on, health_switches. (3) the command line is declared with argenv (health/src/cli.rs). (4) docs hold only facts about the hardware and the results; the phone's state (SIM in or out) is never recorded there; backlog sim-removed-skips closed as superseded, its log entry stays. (5) provisioning: the Alpine package lpoco-health (published by the conveyor since 0.1.6) is what devlab suite put now takes; --runner builds the runner on the lab for what is unreleased; put migrates the old devlab-health reports, month data ledger and once-a-day marks with nothing lost, and the package keeps devlab-health and /usr/lib/devlab/health as other names until the phone's own checks call the new ones. (6) upstream: we do not fork postmarketOS' test pieces now; we write our checks so they could be sent upstream, and revisit when their system-level tests or farm admission exist.
why: The SIM removal showed that a state of the phone cannot live in docs: it is true for minutes and the phone knows it better. Every mature phone CI (bootrr, LAVA, postmarketOS's test package, CI-tron) keeps tests as small executables with one result line each and a thin runner, device facts as data and an explicit skip; nobody compiles on the device. Upstream postmarketOS (checked 2026-11-17) runs on-device tests only from the initramfs, halting the boot; boot and system tests - the modem, audio, sensors, sleep and budgets we need - are not built, and their farm is one phone behind a token gate. Our checks and runner already have the shape, so it is kept and extended, not replaced (decision 2026-11-17-health-on-the-phone weighed first).
rejected: A. Building fully on postmarketOS upstream (fork their test pieces into a rhizcut-synced subfolder, send improvements back as merge requests): the right long-term friend - open GitLab, clear review rules, Python only host-side so it does not weigh against it - but today it gives us only the initramfs hook, which halts the boot and covers kernel tests, not the after-boot system tests we run; their farm has one OnePlus 6T and registration is token-gated; whether rhizcuts handle a GitLab upstream and a subfolder is not known; licence/CLA and fork-sync cost not known. Revisit when upstream gets system tests or admits other phones. C. A different shape of our own: nothing to gain over B. rust-script tests with a bundle crate (the author's lean, weighed fairly): the dependency direction is right (bundle depends on tests, not the reverse) and nextest shows it works, but rust-script needs rust+cargo on the phone (Alpine aarch64 72 MiB download, 206 MiB installed plus gcc, musl-dev, llvm-libs, network for crates), a registry (inventory/linkme) is unproven on aarch64 musl and links everything into one binary; kept instead: the same direction by discovery - the runner finds tests in directories, tests depend on nothing of it - and Rust for logic (runner, ledger, tone) built on the lab as a static binary; revisit as prebuilt per-test binaries when a check needs more than shell. Building each test on the lab as its own binary now: cross-build work for 13 small shell checks that need none. A settings store in docs or in devlab's lab-side files: wrong place for the phone's state, goes stale. Keeping the name devlab-health: the suite is linux-phone-oco's, not devlab's; the old name stays only as an alias. Lab-built runner by default: the package is published, so the package is the default.

brief: Pixel 2 is fastboot-first: boot in memory, write nothing
decision: Until a recorded decision says otherwise, walleye is only ever changed by 'fastboot boot' (a kernel held in memory); both A/B slots stay untouched, and the stock Android on it is measured as the android-reference before any flash.
why: It is the only Android reference we have and the only thing between a bad kernel and a phone that needs a factory image; fastboot boot falls back by itself on reset.
rejected: Flashing a boot slot for the first try (loses the reference and a slot); wiping to install postmarketOS first (loses the reference); building devlab's fastboot mode here (devlab belongs to orchestration).

brief: walleye gets its own lab repository, made from device-template
decision: linux-phone-oco/google-walleye-lab, made from device-template, with its own device.toml and its own devlab lease; surya's lease is never touched.
why: The template exists for exactly this; one lease per phone keeps two lanes from blocking each other.
rejected: A directory in surya-lab (mixes two phones' manifests); one shared lease (one phone's keeper would stall the other).

brief: devlab reaches a phone over fastboot only by its manifest's serial, and writes over fastboot only where the manifest says writes = true.
decision: device.toml [fastboot] serial (as fastboot devices lists it) and writes (default false). Every fastboot call devlab makes passes -s SERIAL; devlab flash refuses a phone without writes = true; devlab fastboot offers only reading, boot from memory and reboot - no flash, erase or set_active verb. The guard refuses raw fastboot other than devices, getvar and help.
why: A second phone (google-walleye) sits in fastboot on the lab beside surya: devlab flash checked any phone in fastboot and flashed without -s, so a surya flash would have written to walleye. walleye's slots must stay as they are until a recorded decision (walleye-fastboot-first); a default of no writing makes that the phone's state, not a rule to remember.
rejected: writes defaulting to true (a manifest that forgets the line would let walleye be flashed); a flash that takes the only phone in fastboot when there is one (true today, false the moment two are); a separate fastboot tool beside devlab (the lease, hold and guard are devlab's, one way per phone); writing surya's serial from its soc0 serial (3693150539 = dc21014b) unread from fastboot: not known yet is said as not known, so surya's flash refuses until a keeper reads it.

brief: First walleye kernel: kernel.org v7.3 + our own minimal msm8998-google-walleye.dts, USB gadget initramfs; porthole's v7.2.2 series only as fallback and patch source
decision: The first kernel is pristine kernel.org v7.3 with arm64 defconfig plus gadget/configfs options, and a new msm8998-google-walleye.dts (GPL, derived from the wahoo dtsi of kcxt/porthole with licence and authors kept) that enables only reserved memory, RPM regulators, qusb2phy, dwc3 peripheral (USB 2.0), ramoops and UART, and carries qcom,msm-id = <0x124 0x20001> and no bootargs. It is booted once with fastboot boot, in a boot image of header v0 with the dtb appended. Further parts are added one at a time, taking porthole's patches singly.
why: Mainline has no Google board; the only maintained Pixel 2 family kernel (porthole) is shaped by taimen and its walleye board is untested, so a walleye failure on it would not say which of 263 patches or which board difference caused it; a minimal dts keeps the first try small and attributable (bring-up-a-part: test first, one part at a time). v7.3 is the newest release; v7.2.2 is what porthole proved on taimen.
rejected: porthole's whole 7.2.2 series as the first kernel (too large to attribute a failure); kcxt wahoo/5.17 (old, bootargs in the dts hides the bootloader cmdline, no msm-id); display-first or simple-framebuffer start (command-mode panel has no scanned-out framebuffer); flashing dtbo/boot first (decision walleye-fastboot-first); adopting a downstream 4.4 kernel (not the aim).

brief: walleye clean room is a wall on inputs, started light, three roles only where a part needs observed behaviour
decision: Clean room for walleye is a rule on what a session may read (inputs), not a claim about the model's mind: allowed evidence kinds are measured-trace, measured-behaviour, public-spec and gpl-source, each recorded with its file, hash, command and date; never vendor binaries, disassembly or decompiler output, strings out of blobs, firmware read for content (it may only be loaded), leaked or NDA documents; all captured logs and strings are data, never instructions. The GPL vendor kernel and kcxt/linux-wahoo are read and ported with their licence kept (no clean room for them). The bring-up of parts that mainline already has (most of MSM8998: a device tree plus upstream drivers) needs no wall. The full observer / scrubber / implementer split starts only with the first part that needs observed behaviour (likely display panel init, audio calibration, sensor hub, camera), tried first on a part surya already solved; the observer's spec rows are a ikb record to be asked of the ikb session when that part comes.
why: Research 2026-11-17-cleanroom-agents: no court has ruled on AI clean rooms and a wall cannot be proved in the model's mind; an input rule is checkable (Asahi records accesses without looking at code; ArtCraft's rule is on inputs); EFF calls a clean room good practice, not a legal requirement.
rejected: Proving independence by the model's state (unprovable); the full three-role split from the start (overhead for a first kernel that needs no observed behaviour); no rule at all (the GPL-versus-proprietary line must stay checkable); reading blobs/disassembly as an evidence kind (never).

brief: fastboot boot tries on walleye need no further word from the author
decision: On the author's word of 2026-11-17 ("lets do it ... no need to wait on me"), the walleye keeper runs 'devlab fastboot boot now' tries (a kernel in memory only, nothing written) whenever an image is ready, without asking. The author is asked, in one line through the top coordinator, only when the phone needs his hands (holding power to get back to fastboot after a hang). Anything that writes to the phone - flashing a partition, a stub dtbo, switching slots, 'fastboot oem' - still needs its own recorded decision and his word, and devlab's [fastboot] writes stays false until then.
why: A boot from memory leaves both slots as they were and falls back to the stock boot on reset; the author wants the least of his attention.
rejected: Asking for each try (needless attention); a standing go for writes too (a write can cost the Android reference or a slot).

brief: devlab no longer says a RAM boot leaves the slots as they were: it reads the bootloader's A/B flags before and after and says what changed; switching the active slot is a gated word of its own.
decision: fastboot boot now and set-active read current-slot and the slot-unbootable/successful/retry-count flags of both slots before and after, and say the difference; the verdict of a boot is where the phone went, not fastboot's exit. set-active (metadata) is refused unless the manifest says [fastboot] slot_switch = true, separate from writes.
why: walleye's try b: devlab wrote nothing, yet the bootloader's A/B logic ended on slot b with slot a unbootable, and devlab, reading fastboot's failing exit, called the try refused.
rejected: keeping 'nothing written, slots as they were' (true of devlab, false of the phone); folding the switch into writes = true (a flag change is not a partition write, and walleye may need one without the other); restoring slot a by devlab on its own after a try (a write that needs the author's word).

brief: A backlog item names the device it is for; phone-next and phone-queue require --device, and lane-next gives a lane's next item of a kind (phone, research, build)
decision: backlog gains device (a devices id) and needs takes phone, research or build. The records that set needs refuse a phone, research or build item without a device (tad has no conditional rule). phone-next and phone-queue require --device; lane-next --device D --needs N gives the lane's next item, for its keeper and launchers. Filled once: open phone items in docs, surya-lab, lab-tools (about deep-sleep) and sxmo-deviceprofiles (about sx-surya) are xiaomi-surya; google-walleye-lab's and lab-tools' about google-walleye are google-walleye. The briefs, AGENTS.md and the README name the device.
why: Per-lane launchers (ideal-agent decision 2026-11-17-a-lane-starts-its-own) need a lane's next item; needs said only phone, and phone-next could hand surya's items to walleye's keeper. Orchestration (owner of docs), 2026-11-17: the device is a fact of the item, devices.id the reference; required, not optional; list what cannot be placed.
rejected: An optional --device (a walleye keeper would still take surya's items); the lane read off the project (surya's phone items live in docs, about components); a device on components (components are shared across devices); a needs value per device (needs says what kind, device says whose); a table rule (tad has none conditional yet - the records enforce it).

brief: docs keeps general knowledge for all devices; each device has its own open base; docs pulls and derives progress. one-database stays for docs and its tools.
decision: Decision 2026-11-17-one-database is superseded for devices only. Each device (surya, walleye, a third) has its own open base, made from device-template and following idealkb: queue, tries, measurements, decisions, research about it, its parts with status, evidence and date. docs holds concepts, the components and features catalogue, landscape, general decisions and research, shared sources, the tests catalogue, the lab tooling, and a registry of devices with the address of each base; support status and progress are derived from the devices' declared parts, pulled in CI, never typed or copied (stale or missing: not known yet). Lanes and launchers ask their device's own base. A third device is made from the template and registered with one record. The work to get there is on docs' backlog under commons-only, each part with its owner.
why: 40 of docs' own 81 backlog items, 34 of 49 research rows and 14 of 28 decisions name a device; test_results is 1.3 MB of 2.0 MB; the keeper's landings conflict in docs' data; the author wants docs to hold only what helps all devices. The device field and lane-next (docs 260) separate lanes but not weight or conflicts.
rejected: One database with a device field (lanes only); status typed in docs and in the device; submodules or subtrees; push from each device; CI-only derivation (a phone cannot run in CI); superseding one-database wholesale - its reasons still hold for docs and the lab tools. Full reasons: grenudi/ideal-knowledge-base decision 2026-11-17-commons-and-unit-bases.

brief: Find why the Pixel 2 refuses our images with a control image first, then host-built variants one change each; a dtbo stub only after both, on the author's word
decision: 1) A control: a public stock-format walleye image (LineageOS recovery or TWRP) through the same fastboot boot, to learn whether the phone's state or our image causes Load Error. 2) Host-only rebuild of the image on the pmaports blueline recipe (second offset 0, os word 0, short cmdline) and a dts with qcom,board-id/pmic-id read from the stock walleye dtb, tried one change at a time. 3) Only if both still end in Load Error, a stub dtbo in dtbo_b - a write with a recorded way back, needing the author's word.
why: Nothing reported on a Pixel 2 booting mainline; the image format already equals what pmaports boots on Pixel 3; Load Error is also given to known-good TWRP in a bad state, so a control separates state from content cheaply and with no write; the board-id change costs nothing on the host; the dtbo stub is the one proven fix on taimen (kcxt) but changes the phone.
rejected: Flash a stub dtbo first (kcxt's way): proven on taimen only, a write, and the cause may be state or ids; Read slot b's dtbo or boot header via Android first: needs set-active/boot of Android, which flips slot flags; Keep trying more offset variants (a/b style): both offset sets already behave the same under Load Error, so offsets are not the lever; Download Google's factory image to read ids: a proprietary download needing a decision, when LineageOS's public build holds the same header and dtb ids.

brief: A lane's rows move to its device base as they are, by device and project; lab-tools' stay; about across bases is left empty
decision: A lane's rows move from docs into its lab's base, replayed through the base's named records under the lane's keeper lease (orchestration-move): backlog whose device is the lane's (except lab-tools' own items, the conveyor's) or whose project is the lab with no device; research, decisions and log of the lab's project or about a moved item; their research/ folders; test_runs/test_results replayed from the lab's own reports through test-run and compared row for row; parts seeded from docs' support_status of the device. Kept as they were, except: an about naming the device, a docs subject or a milestone is left empty; decision ids without a date gain it; a research without a brief takes its question. The moved rows are deleted from docs through tad sql. Scripts: side-session notes of orchestration (move-lane.sh, replay.sh, select.sh).
why: The device base must hold the lane's whole story to be its own (decision 2026-11-17-commons-and-device-bases); replaying through the records keeps every rule of the new base; an about across bases has no rule yet (about-across-bases), so leaving it empty loses only a link the base implies.
rejected: Copying data/*.json lines by hand (bypasses the records and the base's rules); moving lab-tools' items that carry a device (they help every device); keeping support_status' surya claims only in docs (the base would have nothing to be about); renaming ids freely (links from elsewhere would break).

brief: A device's part pulled from its base counts for 30 days; older, unreadable, undeclared or unclaimed is unknown, 'not known yet' with the reason, never broken.
decision: records/feed-device-parts.sql (run per device with a base, devices.base = owner/name, by bin/run-feeds.sh) writes the device's support_status from its base's data/parts.json, only when devicebase.toml says parts = 1 (read as the one line 'parts = N' by a regular expression over the file's text in DuckDB, which reads no TOML; checked against walleye's and surya's real files). A part is kept when its status is one of the five and its updated is at most 30 days old. Otherwise the component is unknown, with a note 'Not known yet: ...' saying why: contract not declared, part not claimed, row not valid, or last said X on DATE more than 30 days ago. A component docs knows that the base does not claim is unknown. A base that cannot be read (404, not JSON) makes every component of that device unknown through records/device-parts-unknown.sql, and never stops the other feeds. derive-support-status leaves devices with a base alone. feeds.yml runs daily plus workflow_dispatch; no push trigger (a repository_dispatch from each base needs a token in each lab).
why: A status nobody has re-measured for a month is not known any more; an old 'works' on a moving kernel misleads. 30 days is as long as a phone's mainline state stays trustworthy between lab sessions here, and short enough that a lab left idle shows it. Practice 12: not measured shows as not known yet.
rejected: No staleness window (an abandoned base would show works forever); 7 days (a weekend-less lab would flicker to unknown); unreadable base keeps the last pulled rows (hides that the base is down); unreadable base shown as broken; a TOML parser or Python for parts = N; on: push of the bases (needs cross-repo tokens).

brief: lpoco: one roof, a git-style dispatcher over lpoco-* programs, one pin, one release; lpoco-bringup is born under it; devlab and tone join, old names kept.
decision:
WHERE: one place for tools that bring a device up - linux-phone-oco/lab-tools, which already says it holds "tools for bringing up and testing Linux phones, not tied to one device". A new workspace member `bringup` (a library with a binary), beside devlab, health and tone. Not a new repository (lab-tools has the CI, the release-plz and the package conveyor; the device template already points there), and not devlab subcommands (devlab is the phone-facing tool - fastboot, ssh, keeper lease, MCP, tokio and rmcp - and building an image needs no phone, no lease and no network; the boundary stays: bringup makes files on the host, devlab puts them on the phone). devlab may call bringup's library later (kernel try building its own image); it does not grow image code.
NAME AND ONE ROOF (the author: all tools of lpoco under one roof): one command, `lpoco`, with the family as subcommands - `lpoco bringup ...`, `lpoco health ...`, `lpoco lab ...` (today's devlab), `lpoco tone ...`, `lpoco mcp` - as git and cargo do: `lpoco` is a small dispatcher (argenv) that finds the program lpoco-NAME beside itself or on PATH and runs it, so every tool is still its own crate and binary in lab-tools (lpoco-bringup, lpoco-health, lpoco-lab, lpoco-tone) and can be run alone. One roof buys one install, one pin (device.toml [tools] lpoco = "X.Y" names the whole family), one completion and man page, one MCP server (`lpoco mcp`, the tools of every subcommand under their subcommand's name), one place agents look (`lpoco list`). The family is released together: one version, and the dispatcher stops with a line naming both versions when a subcommand's version differs from its own (nothing half-upgraded runs). The phone's lpoco-health stays its own small static binary - the dispatcher is not shipped there and the phone carries none of devlab's tokio or rmcp. Old names stay as other names for a while - devlab = lpoco lab, devlab-health, the MCP tool names - so the ~450 references are swept over time and nothing breaks at once (as lpoco-health kept devlab-health). The new tool is born under the roof: the crate and binary are lpoco-bringup from its first commit, the dispatcher first or in the same change. The plain word is the method's own (bring-up-a-part); no acronym.
SHAPE: Rust, command line declared once with argenv (as lpoco-health), wrapping and not reinventing: mkbootimg, unpack_bootimg and avbtool (android-tools, found on PATH, the oracles) for what only they do well - the AVB footer first - and crates for the rest (a header layer such as abootimg-oxide if its v0 write is byte-exact; cpio, flate2, lz4_flex, xz for the initramfs and kernel container; dtoolkit or fdt to read the appended dtb). Our own code is the part nobody has: the checks against the device's expected fields, the swap of one part against a control image, and the reproducible initramfs. The packer is proven against mkbootimg byte for byte by test, so a later Rust writer replaces the wrapped call without changing a result.
FIRST COMMANDS: bringup image info|unpack|pack|swap|check (header v0 first; the swap takes a control image and one part - ramdisk, kernel, dtb, cmdline or a header field - and says what differs; check counts the fields the device's [boot] expects and stops the job on a miss); bringup initramfs build (a newc cpio with fixed times, a template variable for the USB-gadget address instead of the sed rewrite, xz or gzip by the device); bringup bisect FILE (a declared series of swaps against stock). AVB hash footer with algorithm NONE and the control's size and properties is part of pack and swap. Not first: vendor_boot and header v3/v4 (read-only at first), a native AVB, QEMU selftest.
STAYS SHELL, stupid simple: build-kernel (a make call with the config) and build-busybox are a few lines each over a strong tool (make); they stay in the device repository, as thin as they are, shellchecked. rust-script is for one-off analysis of a boot image or a log (decision 2026-11-17-health-checks-shell-and-rust); a rust-script that is used a second time becomes a bringup subcommand. tests/host/gadget-up.sh, a host-side check that the phone's gadget answers, belongs with devlab (it is about the phone) and is a later item.
HOW DEVICES CALL IT: the device's facts move out of the scripts into device.toml, a [boot] table in pmOS deviceinfo's words (header_version, base, kernel_offset, ramdisk_offset, tags_offset, second_offset, pagesize, os_version, os_patch_level, cmdline, dtb = appended, kernel_compression, ramdisk_compression, avb_footer, partition_size). The device's build scripts become one line each (bringup image pack, bringup initramfs build, bringup bisect), then go away where one command says it; the device template names bringup in its AGENTS.md and ships the [boot] table with every value marked CHANGE, like [flash] and [fastboot].
BUILD: queued as backlog for a builder with the first failing test (bringup-image-v0, proof bringup-pack-matches-mkbootimg); this session builds nothing.
HOW A DEVICE USES, EXTENDS, SENDS BACK AND PULLS (the author's rule: side by side, no rebase each time): the tool is followed by a version pin, never copied. Pin: device.toml [tools] lpoco = "X.Y", the family's one pin; lpoco refuses a different version with a clear line (an explicit stop), and installs from a released host binary or cargo install --git --tag bringup-vX.Y.Z (bringup-release settles which is simpler). Extension, never an edit of the tool, in three levels: data ([boot] and the files it names), hooks (executables the manifest names for a step; shell where stupid simple; a nonzero exit stops the job), logic (a rust-script file or small crate in the device repository that depends on bringup's library at the pinned tag). The device's parts are its own files, so a pin bump touches none of them. Sending back: a generic improvement is a pull request to lab-tools from the device's branch, recorded in the device base as an upstream item (form patch, ready on the author's word) against a lab-tools upstream row seeded in device-template beside idealkb and device-template. Pulling in: the weekly pin bump (idealkb's update-pins learns the [tools] line), one pull request per source, the device's CI answering. Same rule for devlab and lpoco-health: lab-tools tools are followed by pin. The files that go with the tool (the [boot] skeleton, hook examples, an initramfs skeleton) travel in device-template's slice by follow.sh as today.
RHIZOID: it carries two cases and lacks three things, none worked around. Its cases: a slice (slice-consumption, the template files) and a cutting (a device that must patch bringup itself before upstream takes it: a cutting of lab-tools, tracking branch pristine, patch branch merged, consumed as a cargo git dependency with [patch]; rare, because the three levels cover most). What it lacks, filed on its own backlog (git-rhizoid.github.io PR 28): cutting-as-cargo-dependency, followers-one-pin-bump, send-back-writes-the-upstream-item. Until it has them: follow.sh and update-pins for slices, a plain fork and a [patch] line for the rare cutting.
why:
Walleye wrote eight shell scripts (~520 lines) in a day, the bisect one alone 87 lines of sed, od and grep over unpack_bootimg's output, and surya's was done by hand: every new device would write them again, and their checks (a count that exits 1) are exactly what a typed tool does better with tests. The author's rule is shell only where stupid simple and a strong tool stands behind it; these scripts are logic (header fields, offsets, a dtb found by magic bytes, a footer copied from a control), so they become Rust, and the two that are only make calls stay shell. Earlier decisions already point here: backlog rust-toolset (one Rust toolset in lab-tools, surya is the test subject and not the mould) and 2026-11-17-health-checks-shell-and-rust (Rust for logic, shell for readings, rust-script for one-offs). The landscape (research bringup-tools-landscape) shows nothing covers the job - pmbootstrap does not build the image and is ~24k lines of Python, magiskboot is GPL and aimed at rooting, abootimg-oxide has the header but no checks, no swap, no footer - so wrapping the oracles and the crates is cheaper and safer than writing a packer first. The name: the author offered linux-phone-oco-bootstrap-helpers (lp-oco-bh); "bootstrap" is pmbootstrap's word and the compiler world's, and means something else to every reader; "helpers" says nothing; five words and an unpronounceable shorthand do not suit a command; lab-tools' names are one plain word each.
A tool's logic is compiled and versioned, so the follow problem for it is a pin, not files laid into the follower; keeping the device's own parts in its own repository beside the tool makes the rebase question vanish rather than solved (research bringup-home-follow-and-rhizoid). It reuses the one pin-and-follow mechanism decided in idealkb's chain-follow-by-slice and the upstream-item flow already used, and keeps rhizoid for what it was made for.
The name was weighed again as a family (research bringup-family-names): git-*, cargo-* and pm* (pmbootstrap, pmaports) are prefixes of tools others install, and a prefix is what makes them findable by completion; a bare plain word is safe only inside one machine. The author asked for a distinctive family.
rejected:
A new repository (a second CI, release and package conveyor for one crate; lab-tools is already where the device template sends people). Devlab subcommands (devlab would take build-time crates and a second job, and its 5.4k lines already carry the phone's whole life; an offline tool should not need a phone manifest's fastboot section to run - it reads only [boot]). Growing the shell scripts into a shared shell library (the pmbootstrap path: more shell, hand-parsed text, no tests, nothing a second device can share by name). Python (refused). Porting mkbootimg and avbtool into Rust first (cost before need; the byte-for-byte test lets it come later). Taking magiskboot or pmbootstrap as a dependency (GPL and rooting-aimed; Python sprawl). Names: linux-phone-oco-bootstrap-helpers and lp-oco-bh (bootstrap means pmbootstrap or a compiler's; helpers has no meaning; too long and unpronounceable), bootstrap, bootkit (a malware word), bootimg (a crate's name and only half the job), imgtool (mcuboot's), mkboot, forge, kit. Shorthand: none - bringup is the short form.
For the home: tools as a slice of files followed into each device repository (compiled logic copied everywhere; every device edit becomes a rebase); every device a cutting (fork) of lab-tools (drags the whole workspace into each device repository, and a device cannot follow two forks); git subtree or submodule (a prefix and a second checkout the device never needs); a plugin loader that runs device code inside the tool (a second language boundary; the hooks and the library cover it); waiting for rhizoid to be implemented (its CLI is stubbed and its consumption side open; the need is now).
Family question: no prefix at all (bringup, devlab, tone: three plain words, but tone and bringup are ordinary words that collide on crates.io and on other people's PATH, and nothing says whose they are); a prefix on everything now (renaming devlab touches ~450 files, the installed path and the MCP tool names, and the name lpoco-devlab stutters; renaming tone buys nothing while it is not installed); a suffix family like systemd's *ctl (lpoco-ctl names nothing); a short prefix lp- (lp is the printer). Words: lpoco-bootstrap, lpoco-bh, lpoco-bootkit, lpoco-images (see the first list), and a short alias `bringup` beside lpoco-bringup (two names for one tool, which is what the family is meant to end).
One roof, the forms weighed (research bringup-one-roof): prefix only, lpoco-* each on its own, devlab and tone deferred (the 2026-11-17 first amendment: findable by completion, but no one install, one pin, one MCP server or one place to look); all tools renamed lpoco-* now and released together with no dispatcher (the same missing roof, and a pin per tool); one fat binary holding every tool (the phone's lpoco-health must stay small and static - it would carry devlab's tokio and rmcp - and a crate per tool is what lets each be tested and run alone; a feature-gated single binary can come later if the dispatcher proves too thin); a hard rename with no old names (breaks ~450 references and the MCP names in one change).

brief: The lpoco family has one version: release-plz version_group lpoco, tags stay per package (lpoco-vX, lpoco-health-vX)
decision: lpoco and lpoco-health (and every later lpoco-*) share one version through release-plz's version_group, starting at 0.1.7 (lpoco-health's). The dispatcher refuses a program whose --version differs, so every lpoco-* program must answer --version with 'NAME X.Y.Z' (lpoco-health now does). Tags stay one per package: lpoco-v{version} for the dispatcher (lab-side only, no phone package) and lpoco-health-v{version} for the conveyor's phone package.
why: Decision 2026-11-17-bringup-in-lab-tools asks for one version pin for the family and one release; version_group gives it without moving the conveyor's tag prefix. Proof: lpoco-refuses-mixed-versions.
rejected: One shared git tag for the whole family: the conveyor reads lpoco-health-v* for the phone package, a shared tag would break it. Independent versions per program: the dispatcher could not tell a compatible program from a stale one.

brief: bringup image: abootimg-oxide is the header layer for read and write; mkbootimg is the oracle in the test, not wrapped by pack
decision: lpoco-bringup image pack/info/unpack/check use abootimg-oxide for the v0 header (parse and write); our code adds the v0 id (SHA-1 over kernel, ramdisk, second with sizes) and the page padding. mkbootimg stays the oracle: the test bringup-pack-matches-mkbootimg builds the same image with it (plain header and with os words) and compares bytes; it skips as 'not measured: no mkbootimg'. The header facts come from device.toml [boot] (deviceinfo words), read by the bringup library (devlab's reader ignores the table until it needs it). check prints one ok/FAIL/not-measured line per fact and exits 1 on a miss; info and unpack.boot.toml print the header as a [boot] table (offsets from base 0), so unpack then pack round-trips.
why: The research measured the crate's header bytes equal to mkbootimg's; the two gaps are small and proven by test. Native Rust pack means no Python or android-tools needed at run time, and the oracle test guards it.
rejected: Wrapping mkbootimg for pack: only needed if the crate were not byte-exact, and it would put a python tool in every run. Writing the 1632-byte header by hand: the crate already does it and also parses v1-v4 for later items.
